Number Of Engines.note:
Count of engines.

Number of engines:
- Open the final New Mexico Environment Department air permit 10681 at https://cloud.env.nm.gov/resources/_translator.php/NWFjY2UwMjdjMmQwODZiNzdjZjc0OTYzNF8yMzgzOTA~.pdf and find Section A603, Engines. It says Westside Station has 'six (6) Jenbacher JGC620 4-Stroke Lean Burn engines' and 'ten (10) Jenbacher JGC624 4-Stroke Lean Burn engines', which is 16 engines.
- The department's completion letter of the application at https://cloud.env.nm.gov/resources/_translator.php/YWJiZTRjNjliM2IwY2NkNGQ1YzM0NWU4Yl8yMzgzODc~.pdf says the same in its project description.
- The permit was issued January 22, 2026. The Statement of Basis at https://cloud.env.nm.gov/resources/_translator.php/ZjIxMzI5OGU3OWMxZTliZGY4YmJlZThmNV8yMzgzODU~.pdf lists the engines as units E-1 to E-16.

milestones.note: The air permit application is dated September 10, 2025.

Status.note:
This re-checks the status and adds a source.

Status:
- The EIA-860M table for September 2026 at https://www.eia.gov/electricity/data/eia860m/xls/september_generator2026.xlsx, sheet Planned, plant 70261 Westside, generators WS01, WS02 and WS03, shows status 'Under construction, less than or equal to 50 percent complete'. That matches the current status construction.
- I did not find a dated start of work, so no construction milestone is given. The earliest dated step found is the application of September 10, 2025.

Backup Power.note:
Backup Power stays no.

Where to find it:
- Open the air permit at https://cloud.env.nm.gov/resources/_translator.php/NWFjY2UwMjdjMmQwODZiNzdjZjc0OTYzNF8yMzgzOTA~.pdf and go to Section A103 or A600, the facility description. It says the engines 'supply electricity to the power grid during peak demand periods'. So this is a grid peaking plant and not a backup supply.

units.notes: The permit confirms 16 engines, six J620 and ten J624. I found no dated start of construction, and no source names an operator. Latest Activity is left alone because the project is moving: permit issued January 22, 2026 and EIA shows it under construction. The engines have two different sizes, so one capacity per engine is not given.

qa.question: Should Westside capacity stay at 63 MW when EIA lists 60 MW?
qa.finding: The EIA-860M table for September 2026 lists three generators of 16, 24 and 20 MW, which is 60 MW. GEM has 63 MW, which is six 3 MW engines plus ten 4.5 MW engines. The permit gives engine power only in horsepower.
qa.recommendation: Leave 63 MW as is unless a document gives the electrical rating of the generator sets. Ask the PM whether to use the EIA 60 MW.
qa.note: EIA file: https://www.eia.gov/electricity/data/eia860m/xls/september_generator2026.xlsx, sheet Planned, plant 70261, rows WS01 16.0, WS02 24.0, WS03 20.0 MW, planned operation March 2027, January 2028 and May 2028. The permit https://cloud.env.nm.gov/resources/_translator.php/NWFjY2UwMjdjMmQwODZiNzdjZjc0OTYzNF8yMzgzOTA~.pdf shows the J620 at 3,713 horsepower and the J624 at 5,771 horsepower in the original table, and 4,581 and 6,161 horsepower in the Statement of Basis at https://cloud.env.nm.gov/resources/_translator.php/ZjIxMzI5OGU3OWMxZTliZGY4YmJlZThmNV8yMzgzODU~.pdf. Neither states electrical MW as a clear figure. I did not find a Jenbacher data sheet in the budget.
